name: Loxapine (Adasuve Inhalation; Oral Loxapine)
summary: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic used for acute agitation (inhaled Adasuve) and schizophrenia (oral). Inhaled loxapine can calm agitation within minutes, but it carries a serious bronchospasm risk and must be given in a certified setting.
description: Loxapine is a typical antipsychotic that can rapidly reduce agitation when inhaled (Adasuve) and can treat schizophrenia when taken orally. The inhaled form has a real bronchospasm risk that can lead to respiratory distress or respiratory arrest—so it’s only given in certified health care settings with emergency airway support and a rescue inhaler on site. Oral loxapine can cause sedation, movement side effects (EPS), low blood pressure, and other antipsychotic risks like neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS).
patient_summary: Inhaled loxapine (Adasuve) is designed for fast calming of acute agitation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder—often within about 10 minutes. The tradeoff: it can trigger dangerous bronchospasm, especially in people with asthma or COPD, so it must be administered in a certified setting with monitoring and a rescue bronchodilator available. Oral loxapine is used for schizophrenia and is titrated over days to weeks based on response and side effects.

primary_indications: Acute agitation associated with bipolar I disorder (inhalation)

linked_conditions.context: Oral loxapine is used to treat schizophrenia. Some experts prefer second-generation antipsychotics first due to potentially fewer extrapyramidal symptoms, but efficacy differences are not consistent across patients.
Inhaled loxapine is used for the acute treatment of agitation associated with bipolar I disorder in adults when rapid calming is needed in a supervised setting.
Inhaled loxapine is intended for fast de-escalation of acute agitation associated with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder, administered only by health care professionals with post-dose monitoring.

contraindications: Inhalation: Current diagnosis or history of asthma, COPD, or other lung disease associated with bronchospasm
Inhalation: Acute respiratory signs or symptoms (eg, wheezing)
Inhalation: Current use of medications to treat airways disease (eg, asthma/COPD meds)
Inhalation: History of bronchospasm following loxapine treatment
Inhalation: Known hypersensitivity to loxapine, amoxapine, or any component of the formulation
Oral: Hypersensitivity to loxapine or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.metric: Time to initial calming effect (inhalation for agitation)
efficacy_response.patient_text: The inhaled form is designed for speed: many patients start to feel de-escalation within about 10 minutes. The goal is rapid calming in a supervised medical setting, not long-term symptom control.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Agitation (inhalation): initial effects within ~10 minutes; Oral/IM: within ~30 minutes for acute effects; Schizophrenia (oral): early benefit may appear in 1-2 weeks with continued improvement over 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: biphasic (initial ~5 hours; terminal ~19 hours); Inhalation: ~6 to 8 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic demethylation and hydroxylation to active metabolites (including desmethylloxapine/amoxapine and hydroxy-metabolites), followed by conjugation

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Loxapine is a first-generation antipsychotic used in psychiatry for two main lanes: (1) fast, supervised calming of acute agitation (inhaled Adasuve) in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder, and (2) ongoing treatment of schizophrenia (oral loxapine). The inhaled version is NOT a take-home inhaler—it’s a controlled, monitored medication because of bronchospasm risk.
items: {link:condition:acute-agitation:Acute agitation}: Rapid de-escalation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder (inhalation, supervised setting only)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone responds differently, but these are the patterns that show up again and again—especially when loxapine is used for agitation or when oral dosing is being titrated:

quotes: It didn’t erase my problems—it just took the edge off fast enough to stop the spiral.
I went from ready-to-explode to… okay. Not euphoric. Just calmer.
It felt like my brain finally got a brake pedal.
items.note: Inhaled loxapine is designed for speed in a supervised setting—often within minutes.

quotes: I felt heavy, like my body wanted to sit still.
My thoughts got quieter, but I also felt kind of foggy.
Calm came with a side of sleepiness.
items.note: Sedation is common and can affect driving, coordination, and decision-making.

quotes: My throat felt irritated, like I’d inhaled something dry.
items.note: Dysgeusia (taste disturbance) and throat irritation are reported with inhaled dosing.

quotes: My chest felt tight and I started wheezing—staff jumped on it fast.
I didn’t realize my breathing was changing until someone checked me.
I felt short of breath and it got scary quick.
items.note: Bronchospasm can be serious. This is why inhaled loxapine is restricted to certified settings with rescue bronchodilator access and monitoring.

quotes: I couldn’t sit still—like my legs had their own agenda.
My muscles felt stiff and my body felt ‘off.’
Restless, jittery, and uncomfortable in my own skin.
items.note: EPS (akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism) can happen, especially with dose increases or higher doses.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: How quickly loxapine works depends on how it’s given and what you’re treating. Inhalation is built for speed. Oral treatment is slower and more about steady symptom control.
key_points: Inhalation (agitation): Initial calming effects can begin within ~10 minutes
Oral/IM: Acute effects may be felt within ~30 minutes; peak effect ~1.5 to 3 hours
Schizophrenia (oral): Early improvement may show up in 1-2 weeks, with continued gains across 4-6 weeks
Duration (oral/IM): Roughly ~12 hours of clinical effect for many patients
Half-life: Oral has a biphasic pattern (initial ~5 hours; terminal ~19 hours); inhalation ~6 to 8 hours

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Speed of calming in acute agitation (inhalation)
sections.text: For acute agitation associated with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder, inhaled loxapine is used because it can calm quickly in a supervised clinical setting. For schizophrenia, oral loxapine is a maintenance-style medication—benefit typically builds over the first few weeks, with continued improvement across the first month or two.
sections.clinical_details: Inhaled loxapine is selected when rapid de-escalation is clinically necessary and monitoring is available. Oral loxapine is titrated gradually to balance symptom control with tolerability, especially sedation, orthostasis, anticholinergic effects, and movement side effects.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Inhaled loxapine can cause bronchospasm that may lead to respiratory distress or respiratory arrest—especially in people with asthma/COPD or other reactive lung disease.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Loxapine is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.
other: Bronchospasm risk (inhalation): Only administer in a certified health care setting with immediate access to a short-acting bronchodilator (eg, albuterol), trained staff, and emergency assistance
REMS restriction (inhalation): Available only through a restricted program under a REMS (Adasuve REMS) to mitigate bronchospasm risk
Sedation/CNS depression: Can impair alertness, coordination, and judgment; sedation can also mask early breathing problems after inhalation
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia: Risk increases with dose and vulnerability factors; monitor closely during titration
Orthostatic hypotension/syncope and fall risk: Higher risk in older adults and during initiation or dose increases
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Rare but life-threatening—fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Blood dyscrasias: Leukopenia/neutropenia/agranulocytosis reported; higher concern with preexisting low WBC or prior drug-induced neutropenia
Aspiration risk: Antipsychotics can be associated with dysphagia/esophageal dysmotility; risk rises with age and frailty
Seizure threshold: Use caution in patients at risk for seizures (history of seizures, head trauma, brain injury, alcohol use disorder, or other pro-convulsant meds)
Catatonia caution: Antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen psychosis and increase NMS risk in catatonic patients
patient_counseling: Inhaled loxapine is not a home medication. It must be given in a certified setting with monitoring and a rescue bronchodilator ready to go.
Before inhaled dosing, clinicians should screen for asthma/COPD or any lung disease with bronchospasm risk, check for wheezing, and assess breathing (including listening to the lungs).
After inhaled dosing, expect to be monitored for bronchospasm symptoms. Tell staff immediately if you feel chest tightness, wheezing, coughing, throat swelling, or shortness of breath.
With oral loxapine, don’t drive or operate machinery until you know how sedated or slowed down you get.
Report muscle stiffness, high fever, confusion, severe restlessness, or uncontrollable movements right away—those can be emergency-level side effects.
If you’re older (especially 65+), the risks of falls, confusion, and movement side effects rise—dosing should start low and be titrated slowly.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Inhaled loxapine commonly causes taste disturbance and sedation, and it can cause respiratory distress in susceptible patients. Oral loxapine carries typical antipsychotic risks: sedation, orthostasis, anticholinergic effects, EPS (including akathisia and tardive dyskinesia), and rare but serious reactions like NMS and blood dyscrasias.
plain_language_list: Dizziness or low blood pressure when standing
Constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, trouble urinating (anticholinergic effects)

common.patient_note: This can hit immediately after inhalation—unpleasant but usually not dangerous. It’s one of the most common ‘yep, that happened’ effects with Adasuve.

Sedation can be helpful when agitation is the problem, but it can also impair coordination and decision-making. It can also make it harder to notice early breathing changes after inhalation—so monitoring matters.

common.incidence: Asthma patients: 54%; COPD patients: 19% (includes bronchospasm, chest pain, cough, dyspnea, pharyngeal edema, wheezing)
common.patient_note: This is the reason for the REMS and certified-setting requirement. Any wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath after inhalation is treated as urgent.
Feeling lightheaded or faint—especially when standing—can happen. It’s more likely if you’re dehydrated, on blood pressure meds, or sensitive to orthostasis.
A scratchy, irritated throat can show up after inhalation. Usually mild, but report any swelling sensation, especially if breathing feels affected.

serious: Bronchospasm (inhalation): can progress to respiratory distress or respiratory arrest; requires immediate bronchodilator treatment and emergency support if severe
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability—medical emergency
Severe blood dyscrasias: leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis (sometimes fatal); stop if significant decline or ANC < 1,000/mm3
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible involuntary movements; risk increases with cumulative exposure and vulnerability factors
Seizures: risk is higher in predisposed patients or with interacting medications/substances
Severe EPS: acute dystonia, severe akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism; can be intensely distressing and may require medication changes
Aspiration pneumonia risk: especially in older adults or those with swallowing difficulties

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Loxapine has meaningful interaction risk through additive side effects (sedation, hypotension, anticholinergic load, EPS, and seizure threshold effects). It is a minor substrate of CYP1A2/CYP2D6/CYP3A4, so the biggest day-to-day issues are usually pharmacodynamic (how effects stack) rather than dramatic metabolism swings.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds)
items.risk: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, falls, confusion, and respiratory risk—especially dangerous when inhalation monitoring is already focused on breathing safety.
items.action: Avoid stacking sedatives when possible. If combination is clinically necessary, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

items.with: Antihypertensives or meds that lower blood pressure
items.risk: Increased risk of orthostatic hypotension and syncope.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms, especially early in treatment and during titration.

items.with: Anticholinergic medications (eg, diphenhydramine, benztropine, many TCAs, some bladder meds)
items.risk: Higher constipation/ileus risk, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth, and delirium risk—especially in older adults.
items.action: Keep the anticholinergic load as low as possible. Monitor bowel/bladder function and cognition.

items.with: Medications that lower seizure threshold (including some antidepressants, stimulants, bupropion, tramadol)
items.risk: Higher seizure risk in predisposed patients.
items.action: Use caution in seizure-prone patients; minimize other seizure-threshold-lowering exposures when possible.

items.risk: Increased risk of extrapyramidal symptoms due to combined dopamine blockade.
items.action: Avoid concomitant use where this contraindication applies; choose alternatives when possible.

items.risk: Potential for modest changes in drug levels due to CYP1A2 effects; clinical impact varies by patient.
items.action: If smoking status changes, reassess side effects and response rather than guessing—adjust if clinically needed.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: For chronic psychiatric illness, stopping antipsychotic treatment abruptly can backfire—either with symptom relapse or with physical withdrawal-type symptoms. If loxapine needs to be stopped and there isn’t a dangerous adverse effect forcing an immediate stop, the safest move is usually a gradual taper over weeks to months with close monitoring.
key_points: In chronic conditions, switching to another antipsychotic is often preferred over simply discontinuing if the goal is ongoing symptom control.
If stopping is necessary, taper the oral dose gradually over several weeks to months when possible to detect early relapse and reduce withdrawal reactions.

Possible withdrawal or rebound symptoms can include: agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, irritability, tremor, restlessness, paresthesias, alternating warmth/chills, myalgias, dyskinesias, and return/worsening of psychosis.

There is no single perfect universal switching strategy. Common approaches include cross-titration (overlap while one decreases and the other increases) or a more abrupt switch depending on relapse risk and side-effect urgency.
If relapse risk is high, clinicians may keep the current medication stable while the new medication is brought to a therapeutic dose, then taper the old one over 1-2 weeks (or longer if needed).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing depends on the formulation and clinical goal. Inhaled loxapine is for one-time acute agitation dosing in a certified medical setting. Oral loxapine is titrated for schizophrenia based on response and side effects.

adult.agitation_inhalation: 10 mg by inhalation once for acute agitation associated with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder (administered by a health care professional in a certified setting)
adult.agitation_im_canada_prn: 12.5 to 50 mg IM every 4 to 12 hours as needed based on response and tolerability (Canadian product)
adult.schizophrenia_oral_initial: 10 mg PO twice daily; if first episode psychosis, consider 5 mg PO twice daily due to higher sensitivity to adverse effects
adult.schizophrenia_oral_titration: Increase total daily dose in increments of 10 mg every 3 to 5 days based on response and tolerability
adult.schizophrenia_oral_typical_range: Usual range: 20 to 100 mg/day in 1 or 2 divided doses

sections.simple_explanation: Inhaled loxapine is a rapid, single-dose option for acute agitation—but it must be given in a certified setting because of bronchospasm risk. Oral loxapine is a scheduled medication used to manage schizophrenia over time, with gradual titration to balance benefit with side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Loxapine is an antipsychotic, so special-population decisions are about balancing psychiatric stability with safety risks. The inhaled form adds a hard stop for many patients: asthma, COPD, or active respiratory symptoms make inhaled loxapine a no-go due to bronchospasm risk.
sections.pregnancy: Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics do not show a large, consistent increase in major congenital malformations, but outcomes vary by study and individual agent data are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can increase the risk of newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (eg, agitation, feeding issues, tone changes, somnolence, tremor, respiratory distress). Treatment decisions should use shared decision-making, prioritize the lowest effective dose of a single agent, and avoid polytherapy when possible. Do not taper late in pregnancy solely to reduce newborn symptoms if it risks maternal relapse.
sections.lactation: It is not known if loxapine is present in human milk. The decision to breastfeed during therapy should weigh infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the benefits of treatment to the parent. If breastfeeding while treated, clinicians typically monitor the infant for sedation, feeding problems, and abnormal tone or movement symptoms.
sections.pediatrics: Avoid in patients ≤18 years when possible due to higher risk of acute dystonic reactions and hyperprolactinemia concerns. Use requires specialist oversight and strong justification.
sections.geriatrics: High-risk medication in older adults. Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic strategies fail and there is risk of harm. Antipsychotics increase stroke risk, cognitive decline, and mortality in dementia. If used for appropriate indications (eg, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), start at the low end of adult dosing, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for orthostasis, falls, sedation, EPS, and hyponatremia/SIADH concerns.
sections.hepatic: Inhalation: No dosage adjustment necessary. Oral: Manufacturer labeling does not provide a specific adjustment; use cautious titration and monitor for sedation, orthostasis, and adverse effects.
sections.renal: Inhalation: No dosage adjustment necessary. Oral: Manufacturer labeling does not provide a specific adjustment; monitor clinically.
sections.respiratory_disease: Inhaled loxapine is contraindicated in patients with asthma, COPD, other lung disease associated with bronchospasm, active wheezing, acute respiratory signs/symptoms, or those using medications to treat airways disease. These patients are at increased risk of serious bronchospasm.
sections.dementia_related_psychosis: Not approved. Increased mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Inhalation-specific: Monitor for signs and symptoms of bronchospasm for at least 1 hour after administration; ensure immediate access to a short-acting bronchodilator (eg, albuterol) delivered by inhaler (with spacer) or nebulizer
Respiratory screening before inhalation: Screen for asthma/COPD/other lung disease, ask about symptoms, assess for respiratory signs, and perform chest auscultation
Mental status and alertness: Every visit; assess sedation, confusion, and functional impairment
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): Every visit; reassess 4 weeks after initiation and dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia: Every visit observation and at least annual structured assessment (more frequent if high risk factors present)
Vital signs: Blood pressure (including orthostatics), pulse, temperature as clinically indicated; watch for syncope, dehydration, autonomic instability, and infection signals
Falls risk: Evaluate regularly in adults ≥60 and anyone with orthostasis/sedation; reassess after dose increases

CBC: As clinically indicated; monitor more frequently early in therapy if preexisting low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; discontinue if significant blood dyscrasia or ANC <1,000/mm3

Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI every visit for first 6 months then quarterly; fasting glucose/HbA1c at ~4 months then annually; lipid panel at ~4 months then annually; assess metabolic syndrome history annually
Electrolytes/renal/liver/TSH: As clinically indicated based on symptoms, comorbidities, and adverse effect concerns
Prolactin: Ask about symptoms (menstrual changes, libido changes, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, sexual function) at visits until stable; check level if symptomatic
Ocular effects: Eye exam as clinically indicated, especially if visual complaints or comorbidities that affect sight

Therapeutic drug monitoring (when used): Draw trough just before next dose; therapeutic reference range cited as 5 to 10 ng/mL, but dosing should be guided by clinical response and tolerability rather than chasing a lab number

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Loxapine comes in different formulations with different use-cases. The inhaled form is a single-use, supervised product for acute agitation. Oral capsules/tablets are for ongoing treatment (most often schizophrenia). Availability can vary by country and product listing status.
items: Inhalation (breath-activated aerosol powder): 10 mg single-use inhaler (Adasuve)
Oral capsules (generic): 5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg
Canada: Intramuscular solution (eg, Loxapac): 50 mg/mL (1 mL)
Canada: Oral tablets (eg, Xylac): 2.5 mg, 10 mg, 25 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Loxapine works mainly by blocking dopamine receptors (especially D2) in brain circuits linked to psychosis and agitation. It also has some serotonin (5-HT2) blocking activity. In plain terms: it reduces dopamine-driven overactivation that can fuel paranoia, disorganization, and agitation—while the tradeoff is a higher risk of movement side effects compared with many newer antipsychotics.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Loxapine sits in two different clinical roles. Inhaled loxapine is a niche, high-supervision tool for rapid calming of acute agitation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder—used when speed matters and monitoring is available. Oral loxapine is a typical antipsychotic option for schizophrenia, but many clinicians consider second-generation agents first because typical antipsychotics can carry a heavier EPS burden. In older adults—especially those with dementia—antipsychotics require extreme caution due to increased mortality and adverse outcomes.

seo.title: Loxapine (Adasuve): Uses for Agitation, Dosing, Side Effects & Bronchospasm REMS
seo.description: Loxapine (Adasuve inhalation; oral loxapine) for acute agitation in schizophrenia/bipolar I and schizophrenia treatment: dosing, fast onset, key side effects (sedation, EPS), and the serious bronchospasm risk requiring REMS-certified administration.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is loxapine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Psychiatry mainly uses loxapine in two ways: (1) inhaled loxapine (Adasuve) for the acute treatment of agitation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder in a supervised medical setting, and (2) oral loxapine for treating schizophrenia over time.

faqs.q: How fast does Adasuve (inhaled loxapine) work for agitation?
faqs.a: It’s designed for speed. Initial calming effects can begin within about 10 minutes. That’s why it’s used for acute agitation when rapid de-escalation matters and monitoring is available.

faqs.q: Why is Adasuve restricted to certified health care settings?
faqs.a: Because inhaled loxapine can cause bronchospasm—tightening of the airways—that can lead to respiratory distress or even respiratory arrest. Certified settings must have trained staff, emergency support, and a short-acting bronchodilator (like albuterol) available immediately.

faqs.q: Can people with asthma or COPD receive inhaled loxapine?
faqs.a: No. Inhaled loxapine is contraindicated in anyone with a current diagnosis or history of asthma, COPD, or other lung disease associated with bronchospasm—and also in patients with acute wheezing or other respiratory signs/symptoms.

faqs.q: What is the usual dose of inhaled loxapine for agitation?
faqs.a: For acute agitation associated with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder in adults: 10 mg by inhalation as a single dose. The maximum is 10 mg per 24-hour period.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of inhaled loxapine?
faqs.a: The most common reported effects include taste disturbance (dysgeusia) and sedation. Throat irritation can also happen. The most serious risk is respiratory distress/bronchospasm in susceptible patients, which is why monitoring is required.

faqs.q: What are common side effects of oral loxapine?
faqs.a: Oral loxapine can cause sedation, dizziness, low blood pressure (especially when standing), anticholinergic effects like constipation/dry mouth/blurred vision, and movement side effects (EPS) like akathisia or stiffness. Rare but serious risks include NMS, blood dyscrasias, and tardive dyskinesia.

faqs.q: Is loxapine approved for dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Like other antipsychotics, loxapine carries an increased mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis and is not approved for that use.

faqs.q: How is oral loxapine dosed for schizophrenia?
faqs.a: A common starting approach is 10 mg twice daily by mouth. For first-episode psychosis, some clinicians start lower (like 5 mg twice daily) because patients may be more sensitive to side effects. The dose can be increased in 10 mg/day steps every 3 to 5 days based on response and tolerability. Usual total daily range is 20 to 100 mg/day (in 1 or 2 doses), with a maximum of 250 mg/day.

If it’s not an emergency adverse effect situation, abrupt stopping is usually a bad idea. Gradual dose reduction over weeks to months can help detect early relapse and reduce withdrawal-type symptoms like agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, restlessness, tremor, and rebound psychosis.

faqs.q: Does loxapine cause movement side effects?
faqs.a: It can. As a typical antipsychotic, loxapine can cause EPS (like akathisia, dystonia, or parkinsonism) and can contribute to tardive dyskinesia with longer exposure. Risk varies by person and increases with higher doses and vulnerability factors.

faqs.q: Is Adasuve something you take at home like an asthma inhaler?
faqs.a: No. Adasuve is not a home rescue inhaler. It’s administered by health care professionals in a certified setting with monitoring and emergency support because of the bronchospasm risk.
